teaser.text: Keurig Dr Pepper is a drinks company with an unusual second engine: it sells branded beverages while also making the coffee machines and pods that turn brewing into a repeat purchase. To understand its business, follow what it sells, who pays, and what remains after ingredients, factories, delivery, overhead and investment take their share.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for KDP?

paragraphs.text: The outcome turns on stabilizing pod demand, cash funding dividends while reducing debt, and JDE Peet’s producing repeatable profit. On November 3, September-quarter results should show U.S. coffee demand and second-half cash generation. By early 2027, both planned companies need independent operations and sound financing. Through the first quarter of 2029, the planned $400 million of synergies must exceed integration and restructuring costs. The investment works only if pod demand stabilizes, cash pays dividends while debt falls, and the separation delivers value.

blocks.heading: What do investors pay for KDP today?

paragraphs.text: The gap between trailing and forward P/E shows how quickly the earnings denominator is changing. The forward measure includes a fuller contribution from the acquisition, while historical profit includes acquisition charges and only a partial contribution. That makes the lower forward multiple attractive only if the added earnings are durable and available to common shareholders.

blocks.heading: Does KDP’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is operating cash after capital spending. In 2025, US$1,991 million of operating cash less US$486 million of capital spending left US$1,505 million, or 9.1% of sales. In 2021, free cash flow was 19.3% of sales. Sales grew, but the cash left after investment fell.

earnings.opening: The next KDP results are expected on November 3, 2026. Watch whether U.S. coffee demand and second-half cash generation improve.

paragraphs.text: KDP’s weighted forecast reaches $42.37 by October 2029, but that outcome hinges on durable earnings, cash conversion, deleveraging and a workable separation. Management guides to $25.9–$26.4 billion of 2026 net sales and 4%–6% constant-currency sales growth for the legacy business. Its 2026 pro-forma leverage ratio is 4.1x.

blocks.heading: Has KDP kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: KDP also has an operating record to test. In February 2025, it targeted mid-single-digit sales growth and high-single-digit adjusted earnings-per-share growth, excluding currency movements. For 2025, it reported 8.6% adjusted sales growth and 7.3% adjusted earnings growth, which management called consistent with guidance. It has not, however, met the original separation timetable: completion moved from the end of 2026 to early 2027.

blocks.heading: What has KDP’s last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: KDP has recently delivered reliably against quarterly expectations. Through June 2026, it beat earnings estimates six times and matched them twice across eight quarters. It beat sales estimates seven times and missed once.

blocks.heading: What should KDP watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: The next scheduled checkpoint is November 3, when KDP reports the September quarter. Investors should look for second-half cash generation, signs of improvement in U.S. coffee, and whether the acquisition is producing repeatable profit rather than timing benefits.
